items.prompt: How does a chameleon's tongue snap out fast enough to catch an insect before it can react?

options.label: The tongue muscles simply contract very hard
options.feedback: Ordinary muscle contraction is far too slow on its own to explain the strike; something is storing energy ahead of time and releasing it all at once.

options.label: The insect is pulled in by a puff of air
options.feedback: A chameleon's mouth creates no vacuum or airflow strong enough to draw prey in from a distance; contact is made by the tongue tip itself.

options.label: Stretched tissue in the tongue releases stored energy all at once
options.feedback: Rings of tissue around a bone in the tongue are stretched taut beforehand; releasing them lets the tongue shoot forward far faster than the tongue's own muscles could contract on their own.

options.label: The tongue is simply longer than the gap to the insect
options.feedback: Length alone would still need to close the gap slowly if nothing sped it up; the strike stands out for its speed, not just its reach.

items.ok_line: Energy loaded in advance, then let go all at once.
items.ko_line: Muscle contracting on its own could never move this fast; something is stored beforehand.
items.exp_title: Energy stored, then released in an instant
items.exp_text: Inside a chameleon's tongue, rings of elastic tissue are wound tight around a bone before the strike, storing energy the way any stretched material does under tension. When the muscle holding that tension releases, the stored energy is unleashed all at once rather than trickling out over the length of a muscle contraction, and the tongue's tip shoots forward far faster than the muscle itself could ever move. A sticky, muscular tip then wraps around the prey the instant it makes contact, before the insect's own reflexes can respond.

items.prompt: How does a spider's web stop a fast-flying insect without snapping?

options.label: The silk stretches and the threads are dotted with sticky glue
options.feedback: Some threads flex and absorb the shock of impact instead of staying rigid, while droplets of glue along them hold the insect fast once its momentum is spent.

options.label: The insect is stunned by the impact alone
options.feedback: Plenty of insects strike a web at only modest speed and still stay caught, so the trap cannot depend on a stunning blow.

options.label: The web is electrically charged to shock prey
options.feedback: Spider silk carries no charge capable of shocking anything; what holds the prey is physical, not electrical.

options.label: The whole web is coated in a single rigid glue
options.feedback: A rigid web would shatter on impact rather than absorbing it; only some threads are sticky, and even those stay flexible.

items.ok_line: Stretch absorbs the hit; glue finishes the job.
items.ko_line: Think about how the threads behave on impact, before anything sticks.
items.exp_text: A web is built from more than one kind of silk: stiff radiating threads form a frame, while the spiral threads that catch prey are far more elastic and can stretch to a good deal more than their resting length. That stretch absorbs the sudden force of an insect flying in, slowing it gradually instead of meeting it with a rigid wall that would simply snap. Regularly spaced droplets of glue along the sticky spiral then hold the slowed insect in place while it struggles.

items.prompt: How does a cuttlefish change its skin colour and pattern in an instant to vanish against its surroundings?

options.label: It reflects light off scales like a mirror
options.feedback: A cuttlefish has no hard scales at all; its skin is soft, and the colour change happens inside that soft skin itself.

options.label: It secretes coloured ink onto its own skin
options.feedback: Ink is squeezed out into the water as a defensive cloud, never spread over the animal's own body to disguise it.

options.label: It slowly grows new pigment over several days
options.feedback: The change happens almost instantly, far too fast to involve growing anything new; existing structures in the skin are simply switched on or off.

options.label: Tiny sacs of pigment in its skin expand and contract
options.feedback: Each sac is surrounded by muscles that can pull it wide open or let it shrink small, and many of these sacs together redraw the pattern almost as soon as the muscles move.

items.ok_line: Muscles pull pigment sacs open or closed, and the pattern shifts on the spot.
items.ko_line: Think about tiny structures inside the skin itself, not something added on top of it.
items.exp_text: A cuttlefish's skin is packed with tiny sacs of pigment, each one ringed by its own set of muscles. Contracting those muscles pulls a sac open wide, spreading its colour across a larger patch of skin, while relaxing them lets the sac shrink back down almost out of sight; different sacs hold different colours, so the mix of open and closed sacs sets the visible pattern. Because muscles can act almost as soon as a nerve signal reaches them, the whole pattern can shift as the animal moves over new ground.

items.prompt: Why does a harmless hoverfly wear the black-and-yellow stripes of a wasp?

options.label: The stripes help it blend into flowers
options.feedback: Bold black-and-yellow stripes stand out against most flowers rather than hiding the insect among them.

options.label: Predators already avoid that pattern, so it borrows the warning
options.feedback: A bird that has been stung once learns to avoid the pattern itself, and a harmless insect wearing the same pattern is avoided right along with the real threat.

options.label: It is a young wasp still growing its sting
options.feedback: A hoverfly is an entirely different insect from a wasp; it never had a sting to grow in the first place.

options.label: The colours simply keep it warm in the sun
options.feedback: Dark and light patches can affect how much heat an insect absorbs, but that would not explain why the pattern matches a stinging insect so closely.

items.ok_line: It never earned the warning; it just wears it.
items.ko_line: Ask what happens the first time a predator meets that pattern on the real, stinging insect.
items.exp_text: A wasp's black-and-yellow pattern advertises a real sting, and any predator that attacks one quickly learns to leave that pattern alone in future. A hoverfly carries no sting at all, but wearing the same bold pattern lets it borrow the lesson the predator already learned, being avoided for a danger it does not actually possess. The resemblance has to be close enough to trigger that learned caution, not perfect in every detail.

items.prompt: How does playing dead protect an animal like an opossum from a predator?

options.label: It confuses the predator's sense of smell
options.feedback: The change here is about behaviour and appearance, not scent; an opossum's smell does not alter when it plays dead.

options.label: It gives the animal time to plan an escape
options.feedback: While playing dead the animal is not alert or planning anything; its body actually enters a state it does not control.

options.label: Many predators lose interest in prey that stops moving
options.feedback: A lot of hunting responses are triggered by motion, so a body that goes still and unresponsive can fail to register as prey worth eating at all.

options.label: It makes the animal look too big to attack
options.feedback: Playing dead makes an opossum go limp and small, not larger; looking bigger is a different defence entirely.

items.ok_line: No movement, no trigger, no attack.
items.ko_line: Ask what a predator's hunting instinct usually responds to in the first place.
items.exp_text: Many predators are triggered to attack, and to keep attacking, mainly by movement and struggle. An opossum that is cornered can enter a state where its body goes rigid, its breathing slows, and it stops responding to touch, sometimes even releasing a foul smell that suggests decay. With no movement to react to and a smell that suggests the meal is already spoiled, a predator that hunts fresh, moving prey often loses interest and walks away.

items.prompt: Why is a poison dart frog brightly coloured instead of camouflaged?

options.label: Bright colour helps predators learn to avoid it quickly
options.feedback: A predator that survives one taste of a brightly marked frog associates the striking pattern with the unpleasant result and remembers to avoid that pattern afterward.

options.label: Bright colour makes the poison stronger
options.feedback: Colour and toxin are produced separately in the body; how bright the frog looks has no effect on how strong its poison is.

options.label: It helps the frog find mates in the dark
options.feedback: These frogs are active by day, when their colour is already highly visible, so a role suited to darkness does not fit.

options.label: It scares off predators by looking larger
options.feedback: The bright pattern does not change the frog's size or shape at all; the message is about danger, not about looking bigger.

items.ok_line: A pattern built to be remembered, not missed.
items.ko_line: Camouflage protects by never being noticed at all; this frog does the opposite. Ask why that might work.
items.exp_title: A colour that teaches a lesson fast
items.exp_text: A camouflaged animal survives by never being noticed, but that only works if nothing ever attacks it in the first place. A poisonous animal can afford the opposite strategy: by advertising itself with a pattern predators can spot and remember easily, it turns each attack that fails into a lesson the predator carries forward. Once a predator has learned to associate that particular look with a bad experience, it avoids anything wearing the same pattern before ever tasting it again.

items.prompt: How do animals that hunt in a coordinated group catch prey too large or fast for one hunter alone?

options.label: Each hunter attacks independently at the same moment
options.feedback: Attacking all at once with no coordination usually lets the prey escape through a gap; the advantage of a group comes from working together, not from timing alone.

options.label: The group simply outnumbers the prey
options.feedback: Numbers alone are not enough if every hunter goes for the prey the same way; how the group divides up the chase matters more than how many hunters there are.

options.label: One dominant hunter does all the work while others watch
options.feedback: In a coordinated hunt, several members typically take active, different roles rather than one doing everything and the rest observing.

options.label: Different members take on separate roles to herd or corner it
options.feedback: Splitting the work — some driving the prey, others waiting to cut off its escape — lets the group overwhelm prey that would easily outrun or outfight any one of them alone.

items.ok_line: Splitting the work turns a hopeless chase into a manageable one.
items.ko_line: Think about what each individual hunter is doing differently, not just how many there are.
items.exp_text: A single hunter chasing fast or dangerous prey head-on often cannot close the gap or risks injury in a direct fight. A coordinated group instead divides the task: some members drive the prey in a chosen direction, while others move ahead to block the escape routes it would otherwise use. By the time the prey is worn down or cornered, the group has spent far less effort per hunter than a lone chase over the same distance would have cost.

items.prompt: How does an ambush hunter like a crocodile catch prey without ever chasing it?

options.label: It gives off a scent that lures prey close
options.feedback: A motionless crocodile relies on staying unnoticed, not on releasing anything that would draw attention to itself.

options.label: It stays motionless until prey comes within a sudden strike
options.feedback: Floating almost invisibly at the surface, it waits for prey to approach on its own, then relies on one explosive lunge rather than a pursuit.

options.label: It digs pit traps prey fall into
options.feedback: A crocodile hunts from open water or a riverbank, not from a concealed pit dug in the ground.

options.label: It swims faster than anything it hunts
options.feedback: Over any real distance a crocodile is outpaced by most of the animals it preys on; a chase is exactly what it avoids.

items.ok_line: Patience does the work a chase never could.
items.ko_line: Think about how a crocodile spends most of its time before prey ever gets close.
items.exp_text: A crocodile spends long stretches almost perfectly still, with only its eyes and nostrils above the waterline, relying on camouflage and patience rather than pursuit. Prey coming down to drink has no reason to notice a shape that never moves, and by the time it is close enough, the crocodile explodes from stillness into a single powerful lunge covering the gap in an instant. Because the whole strategy depends on surprise, a missed strike usually means going back to waiting rather than giving chase.

items.prompt: How do a porcupine's quills defend it without the porcupine ever attacking first?

options.label: They release a toxin into the attacker
options.feedback: Porcupine quills carry no venom or toxin; the defence works through the injury and irritation of the quill itself, not any poison.

options.label: They break off and grow back within minutes
options.feedback: A lost quill takes real time to regrow, and the defence works during the attack itself, well before any regrowth could matter.

options.label: Tiny barbs make them work deeper in with movement
options.feedback: Backward-facing barbs near the tip catch in flesh, so every twitch or movement of the attacker's muscles drags the quill in further rather than letting it slip out.

options.label: They are thrown at attackers from a distance
options.feedback: A porcupine cannot fling its quills through the air; they detach and stay behind only when an attacker actually makes contact with the animal.

items.ok_line: Every movement the attacker makes drives the quill deeper, not out.
items.ko_line: Think about the tip of the quill, not what fills it or how far it travels.
items.exp_title: A barb that works itself deeper
items.exp_text: A porcupine's quills detach easily and lodge in the skin of anything that presses against them, delivering a sharp, immediate pain on contact. Near the tip, microscopic barbs point backward, so instead of sliding back out, a quill catches on surrounding tissue with every movement the attacker makes, and normal muscle motion actually drags it in deeper rather than working it loose. The lingering injury and difficulty of removal teach a lesson that keeps attackers from trying a porcupine a second time.

items.prompt: How does releasing a cloud of ink help a squid escape from a predator?

options.label: It hides the squid's shape and confuses the predator's senses
options.feedback: The dark cloud blocks sight instantly, and in some species it can even be shaped into a rough decoy, all while the real squid jets away in another direction.

options.label: The ink is poisonous to whatever touches it
options.feedback: The ink itself is not what harms an attacker; its purpose is to conceal, not to injure.

options.label: It makes the water too dark for the squid to be eaten
options.feedback: The cloud drifts and thins within moments, so its usefulness comes from confusion in that brief window, not from lasting darkness.

options.label: It sticks to the predator's mouth so it cannot bite
options.feedback: Squid ink is a fine, spreading pigment, not a sticky or gluing substance capable of holding a predator's jaws shut.

items.ok_line: A shadow left behind while the real animal slips away.
items.ko_line: Think about what the cloud does to a predator's senses in that first instant, not afterward.
items.exp_title: A shadow left behind while the real animal flees
items.exp_text: When threatened, a squid releases a cloud of dark ink from a gland near its gut, and the same jet of water it uses to swim helps spread that ink instantly into a screen between itself and the attacker. In many species the cloud even holds together briefly in a shape roughly the squid's own size, giving a predator something solid-looking to strike at. While the attacker's attention is caught on that decoy, the squid jets off in a different direction entirely, well clear before the cloud has even begun to drift apart.
